promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Oct 18 2026, race week, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Your fitness is built, and you ran last week exactly to plan. Heavy legs mean the taper is working, not that fitness is leaving, so skip the 16-miler and start Sunday at 8:40–8:45/mi.

flags.title: No extra miles this week
flags.detail: The 16-miler stays out, and so do extra runs or reps. In September you added running when you felt good, and race week is when that costs the most.

flags.title: Heavy legs should lift
flags.detail: Flat, dead legs are normal in the second week of a taper. They often lift in the last two or three days, as long as nothing hurts.

flags.title: Wednesday stays short
flags.detail: Run the 2 mi at 8:35/mi and stop there, even if it feels easy. The run is there to practise rhythm, not to test your fitness.

flags.title: Race start pace
flags.detail: Hold 8:40–8:45/mi for the first 3 mi. Race-day excitement makes 8:15/mi feel easy, and that costs far more in the last 10K.

answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer:
Yes, skip it. A 16-miler on Wed Oct 14 would still be in your legs on Sunday. A long run takes two to three weeks to turn into fitness, but its fatigue arrives within days, so it would make you more tired without making you more ready.

You're already ready. You've run two 20-milers and a 17. You've also run 4 to 7 miles at marathon pace three times without fading. Your easy runs are still 9:52/mi at 139 bpm, the same as a month ago, so you haven't lost anything.

The dead-leg feeling is the taper doing its job while your body recovers from the big weeks. If you want something on Wednesday that makes you feel ready, the planned 2 miles at 8:35/mi will do that far better than 16 slow miles.

new.analysis:
**You ran last week exactly as planned.** Every run matched its planned distance. The 4 miles at marathon pace on Wed Oct 7 averaged 8:36/mi without fading. You skipped nothing and added nothing, which is a clear change from early September, when extra runs and reps crept in.

**This week keeps your usual pattern but cuts the running to about a third of your biggest weeks.** About 16 miles before Sunday keeps you loose and in rhythm, and it lets the last of the tiredness from the 20-milers clear. The short marathon-pace run and the strides keep some speed in your legs. A taper with no faster running often leaves people sluggish on the start line.

**Under 3:45 is realistic if you pace it evenly.** You've held 8:30–8:40/mi for 4, 6 and 7 miles, and your threshold reps were 7:55/mi. Both fit that goal. Your 10:00/mi long runs still spent about half their time in zone 3, so the last 10K will be hard work, and going out too fast is the easiest way to lose the goal.

**Check the race clock at these points rather than your watch's pace.** GPS usually measures a little long over 26.2 miles, so your watch will show you slightly faster than you really are. These times already allow for the slower first 3 miles.

| Point | Clock time on track for 3:45 |
| --- | --- |
| 10K | about 53:30 |
| Halfway | about 1:52:30 |
| 20 mi | about 2:51:30 |
| Finish | under 3:45:00 |

If you're a minute behind at halfway, don't chase it in one mile. Make it up a few seconds at a time over the next 10 miles.

**Race day should hold no surprises.** Use the same breakfast, gels and drinks you used on your long runs, and try nothing new. Sleep on Thursday and Friday nights matters more than Saturday, so don't worry if nerves keep you up the night before.
